Real analysis

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Analysis
OurBigBook.com Words: 70k Articles: 999
Real analysis studies limits, continuity, differentiation, integration, and convergence of sequences and functions taking values in the real numbers. Its central question is how finite approximations determine an exact answer: what does an arbitrarily small error mean, and which operations respect that error? A derivative is a limit of quotients, while a Riemann integral is obtained from increasingly fine Riemann sums. Both need conditions that make the answer independent of the approximations chosen.
Two organizing ideas are completeness of the real numbers, which ensures that suitable approximations have a destination, and uniform convergence, which controls approximation error over an entire domain. Pointwise convergence supplies separate guarantees at separate inputs; uniform convergence supplies one guarantee for all inputs. This distinction explains why replacing an approximating function by its limit can preserve continuity or integrals under appropriate hypotheses, yet fail without them.
For historical context, Cauchy's 1821 Cours d'analyse explicitly discusses convergence of series. Its Note VII treats double series and compares summing by rows and by columns under stated convergence assumptions: controlling an infinite process was already a concrete problem. This is historical context for questions about limits, rather than an attribution of the modern definitions below. [ref].

Hardy's inequality

Words: 29
Real analysis OurBigBook.com
Hardy's inequality bounds averages or weighted functions by their original size or derivatives. For p>1 and f≥0, its integral form is ∫0∞​(x−1∫0x​f(t)dt)pdx≤(p/(p−1))p∫0∞​f(x)pdx. Spatial weighted forms include the Hardy inequality in Euclidean space.

Infimum and supremum (inf, sup)

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Real analysis OurBigBook.com
For a subset A of a partially ordered set, its infimum is its greatest lower bound and its supremum is its least upper bound. An upper bound only has to lie above every member; the supremum is the smallest such bound. A lower bound lies below every member; the infimum is the largest such bound. These definitions identify the exact edges of a set even when neither edge belongs to it.
For example, (0,1) and [0,1] both have infimum zero and supremum one. Only [0,1] has a minimum and a maximum: those must be actual members of the set. The set C={1/n:n∈N>0​} has infimum zero without a minimum, but its supremum one is also its maximum. Such examples distinguish a bound from an attained extremal value. [ref].
For a nonempty subset of the real numbers, completeness of the real numbers guarantees a real supremum when it is bounded above, and a real infimum when it is bounded below. The bound and the ambient partially ordered set both matter: {q∈Q:q≥0, q2<2} has supremum 2​ in the real numbers, but no supremum in the rational numbers. The detailed explanation belongs to completeness of the real numbers.
Why are unattained bounds useful? They specify a precise limiting target. In mathematical optimization, f(x)=x on (0,1) has infimum zero but no global minimizer. The inputs xn​=1/n for n≥2 give a minimizing sequence: their objective values approach zero without ever reaching it. Bounds therefore describe what approximation can achieve even when no feasible input is best. The approximation property of an infimum and approximation property of a supremum express this idea quantitatively.

Essential infimum and essential supremum (essinf, esssup)

Words: 468 Articles: 1
Infimum and supremum OurBigBook.com
The essential infimum and essential supremum describe the lower and upper bounds of a measurable function after disregarding null sets for a specified measure. A pointwise infimum or supremum sees every input; an essential bound sees whether values below or above a proposed threshold occur on a set of positive measure. Thus "essential" means insensitive to changes on a null set, rather than insensitive to unusual values. This distinction makes essential bounds compatible with Lebesgue integrals and the equivalence classes used in Lp spaces. [ref].
For a real measurable function f on a measure space (X,Σ,μ), the definitions are
essinfμ​f=sup{a∈R:μ({x:f(x)<a})=0},esssupμ​f=inf{b∈R:μ({x:f(x)>b})=0}.
(1)
These can take values in the extended real number line. On a space of positive total measure, finite essential bounds obey essinfμ​f≤f≤esssupμ​f almost everywhere. If s=esssupμ​f is finite, every threshold b<s has μ({f>b})>0; the corresponding lower-edge statement is μ({f<a})>0 for every a>essinfμ​f. These are the measure-based counterparts of the approximation property of a supremum and approximation property of an infimum.
Here is a two-sided example on [0,1] with Lebesgue measure:
g(x)=⎩⎨⎧​−3,4,x,​x=1/4,x=3/4,otherwise.​
(2)
The pointwise bounds are infg=−3 and supg=4, while the essential bounds are essinfg=0 and esssupg=1. Both exceptional singletons are null sets. But for 0<a<1, the inputs where g<a still have measure a, and those where g>a have measure 1−a: deleting or adding two individual inputs cannot change those lengths. Hence neither essential bound can be moved inward.
The choice of measure is part of the answer. The same g has essential bounds −3 and 4 under counting measure, because every nonempty set has positive measure. Under the Dirac measure at 1/4, both essential bounds equal −3. A null set for one measure need not be a null set for another.
Nor must the exceptional inputs be isolated. The Dirichlet function, equal to one at rational numbers and zero at irrational numbers, has pointwise supremum one on [0,1], but essential supremum zero for Lebesgue measure: the rational numbers form a countable set that is a null set, even though they are dense. Conversely, a value ten on an interval of length 0.001 affects the essential supremum just as decisively as it would on half the domain. Small positive measure is not zero measure.

Essential infimum (essinfu)

Words: 92
Essential infimum and essential supremum OurBigBook.com
The essential infimum of a real measurable function is essinfμ​f=−esssupμ​(−f). It is the largest lower bound that holds almost everywhere, with values allowed in the extended real number line. Unlike a pointwise infimum, it is unchanged by altering a representative on a null set.
For the function g in essential infimum and essential supremum, the value −3 at one input changes the pointwise infimum, but the essential infimum remains zero under Lebesgue measure. If instead a function is −3 throughout an interval of any positive length and zero elsewhere, its essential infimum is −3. The distinction concerns the measure of the low-value set, rather than the magnitude of the low value.

Supremum (sup)

Words: 246 Articles: 2
Infimum and supremum OurBigBook.com
For a nonempty set A⊆R, a real number s is its supremum precisely when it is an upper bound and no smaller real number is an upper bound. It is unique: two least upper bounds must each be no greater than the other.
For A=(0,1), every number at least one is an upper bound, and none smaller than one bounds the whole set. Thus supA=1, although 1∈/A. For A=[0,1], that same supremum is also the maximum. The approximation property of a supremum supplies witnesses arbitrarily close to an unattained upper edge.

Approximation property of a supremum (∀ε>0∃a∈A: s−ε<a≤s)

Words: 90
Supremum OurBigBook.com
Let A⊆R be nonempty and bounded above. An upper bound s equals supA exactly when, for every ε>0, some a∈A satisfies s−ε<a≤s. If no such member existed, s−ε would be a smaller upper bound. Conversely, the condition defeats every proposed upper bound u<s by taking ε=s−u. [ref].
For (0,1) and ε=0.2, a=0.9 is one witness: 0.8<0.9<1. Choosing an​∈A with s−1/n<an​≤s produces a sequence converging to s by the squeeze theorem. The choices need not form a monotone sequence.

Accumulation below an unattained supremum

Words: 71
Supremum OurBigBook.com
If a nonempty real set A has finite supremum s and s∈/A, then every interval (s−ε,s) contains infinitely many elements of A. Otherwise its finitely many elements have a largest value m<s; all remaining elements are at most s−ε, making max(m,s−ε)<s an upper bound. The interval cannot be empty either, by the defining approximation property of a supremum. Thus failure to attain a finite supremum forces accumulation from below.

Infimum (inf)

Words: 134 Articles: 1
Infimum and supremum OurBigBook.com
For a nonempty set A⊆R, a real number ℓ is its infimum precisely when it is a lower bound and every other lower bound is at most ℓ. It is the greatest lower bound, not necessarily the minimum.
For C={1/n:n∈N>0​}, zero is a lower bound. Every positive candidate ε fails: the Archimedean property gives an integer n>1/ε, hence 1/n<ε. Thus infC=0, although zero is never a member of C. This is the lower-edge counterpart of approximating an unattained supremum.

Approximation property of an infimum (∀ε>0∃a∈A: ℓ≤a<ℓ+ε)

Words: 57
Infimum OurBigBook.com
Let A⊆R be nonempty and bounded below. A lower bound ℓ equals infA exactly when every ε>0 admits a∈A with ℓ≤a<ℓ+ε. Otherwise ℓ+ε would be a larger lower bound. Taking tolerances 1/n gives a sequence of members converging to ℓ. Asymptotic analysis

Real analysis OurBigBook.com
Asymptotic analysis describes what remains dominant as an argument approaches a specified limit. It compares functions or sequences by scale: how much of a complicated expression can be replaced by a simpler one, and how large is the omitted part? The limit may be n→∞ for a growing input or h→0 for a shrinking approximation parameter.
For example, n2+105n is eventually dominated by its quadratic term, since division by n2 gives 1+105/n→1. But at n=100, the linear term contributes 107, compared with only 104 from the quadratic term. A statement about the limiting scale and a good approximation at a particular input are different claims.
Three useful comparisons keep their strengths distinct. Big O notation supplies an eventual upper bound up to a constant multiplier; big theta notation supplies both an upper bound and a lower bound up to constants; asymptotic equivalence makes the ratio tend to one. Little o notation says that a term becomes negligible relative to a specified scale. These distinctions make approximations checkable instead of merely calling one expression small.
The same language connects time complexity with Taylor remainders. In an operation-count model, one asks how a cost scales with input size. In a Taylor expansion, one asks how the approximation error scales with the increment. Neither use requires interpreting the unspecified constant as one. The asymptotic comparison of exponential functions gives another example: dividing by the largest contributing exponential reveals the terms that disappear.

It is useful when the scaling exponent is stable but a smaller correction continues changing. The correction can even grow without bound.
An eventually positive measurable function q has regular variation at infinity with index ρ∈R if

At t=100,104,106 this is approximately 4.60206,4.30103,4.20069, respectively. The ratio approaches four slowly, even though the exponent is exactly two in the limiting scaling law.
The slowly varying function isolates this correction. Set ℓ(t)=q(t)/tρ. Then

A Pareto distribution gives a decreasing example with a direct interpretation. For x≥1, take the tail probability P(X>x)=x−2. Its regular variation index is −2. Doubling a threshold divides its tail probability by four, and

For a tail probability with regular variation of index −α, the same conditional probability tends to 2−α. An exponential distribution behaves differently: its corresponding conditional probability is e−λt→0. This comparison explains why scaling limits are useful in extreme value theory; it does not establish that an observed dataset follows a particular tail model. The role of regular variation in heavy-tailed distributions is discussed in Lindskog, Resnick and Roy, introduction, p. 1.

Boundedness alone is also insufficient, as the oscillating counterexample in slowly varying function shows. Checking a few rescaling ratios at finite arguments can illustrate a proposed law, but cannot prove its limiting definition.

Words: 1k Articles: 11
Real analysis OurBigBook.com
A function f:X→Y between metric spaces is Lipschitz continuous if one finite number L≥0 controls every change of output by the corresponding change of input:
dY​(f(x),f(y))≤LdX​(x,y)(x,y∈X).
(28)
For real inputs and outputs this is ∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤L∣x−y∣. The same bound must work for every pair in the specified domain of a function. It gives a quantitative version of continuity: an input error of at most ε produces an output error of at most Lε. The least possible bound is the Lipschitz constant. Lebl presents the real and metric-space definitions and their connection with uniform continuity. [ref]
Three functions show why this condition differs from differentiability. The absolute value f(x)=∣x∣ has a corner at zero, but the reverse triangle inequality gives ∣∣x∣−∣y∣∣≤∣x−y∣, so it has Lipschitz constant one on the real line. The sine is smooth and also has Lipschitz constant one: the mean value theorem and ∣cost∣≤1 bound every secant slope. The square root is continuous on [0,1], but
∣h−0∣∣h​−0​∣​=h​1​⟶∞(h↓0).
(29)
No finite Lipschitz bound works on that interval. At h=1,1/4,1/16,1/64, the ratios are 1,2,4,8. Smaller input changes near zero therefore require larger amplification factors.
For a real function, Lipschitz continuity means that the absolute slopes of all secant lines are bounded. If the derivative exists at a point, taking a limit of those slopes gives ∣f′(x)∣≤L. In the other direction, a function that is continuous on a real interval, differentiable in its interior, and satisfies ∣f′∣≤L there is Lipschitz continuous by the mean value theorem. The interval hypothesis matters: the theorem uses the segment connecting the two inputs.
A Lipschitz function is uniformly continuous: for L>0, choosing input tolerance δ=ε/L works at every point. If L=0, the function is constant. The converse fails; the square root on [0,1] is uniformly continuous, and satisfies the weaker Hölder continuity bound ∣x​−y​∣≤∣x−y∣​, without a finite Lipschitz constant. These distinctions are developed in Lebl's worked examples. [ref]
The usefulness is controlled sensitivity. Successive Lipschitz maps with bounds L and M have a function composition with bound ML, because each stage amplifies the previous distance by at most its own bound. For an ordinary differential equation, Lipschitz continuity in the unknown state is the condition that makes nearby trial solutions controllably close in the Picard-Lindelöf theorem. For incomplete data, the McShane extension theorem fills in unobserved values while preserving the same bound. This one inequality connects error estimates, uniqueness, and interpolation.

A function between metric spaces is locally Lipschitz if every point has a neighbourhood on which one finite Lipschitz bound works for every pair. The neighbourhood and bound may depend on the point. A continuously differentiable real function on an open interval has this property: continuity of its derivative bounds that derivative on a sufficiently small closed interval, and the mean value theorem bounds every secant slope there.
The function x2 is locally Lipschitz at every real point but has no single bound on the real line. The square root is locally Lipschitz on (0,∞), and has the bound 1/(2a​) on [a,b] for 0<a<b. Adding zero to its domain changes the conclusion at that point: the ratios in the Lipschitz continuity example become unbounded, so it is not locally Lipschitz at zero. This distinction is what permits the delayed, nonunique ODE solutions illustrated under Picard-Lindelöf theorem.

The same constant must work for all sufficiently large inputs. Near a finite limit point a, replace n≥N by 0<∣x−a∣<δ within the domain. Absolute values allow signed or complex-valued functions; when discussing nonnegative operation counts they can be omitted.
The notation records an upper bound, not an exact leading coefficient or necessarily a tight growth order. For example, 3n2+7n+4=O(n2) because for n≥1 it is at most 14n2. It is also O(n3), a weaker statement. A tight comparison uses big theta notation; a ratio tending to one uses asymptotic equivalence. Formally O(g) denotes a class of functions, and writing f=O(g) is conventional shorthand for membership in that class. [ref]
The first panel compares stipulated operation counts A(n)=1000n and B(n)=n2. Although A is linear and B quadratic, B(n)<A(n) for 1≤n<1000; the ordering reverses beyond their crossing. The time complexity notation describes the growth of whichever cost function has been specified, whether that function represents a worst-case bound, an average, or another explicit quantity.
The middle panel gives a concrete eventual bound: n2+105n≤2n2 for every n≥105. Its normalized ratio approaches one, but the threshold matters. The final panel shows the asymptotic comparison of exponential functions, with its geometrically shrinking relative difference.
Constants may depend on fixed parameters. For each fixed α>0, fα​(n)=αn is O(n) with C=α; one constant cannot cover every positive α. A uniform big O bound makes this extra quantifier explicit.
The notation was already used in nineteenth-century number theory. In his 1976 paper, Donald E. Knuth reports Landau identifying Bachmann's 1894 book as the first appearance of O known to him. Knuth's account gives the earlier mathematical setting of a notation now also common in time complexity analysis. [ref]

A sequence of nested intervals keeps every new enclosure inside the previous one:
I1​⊇I2​⊇I3​⊇⋯.

Each step adds a restriction without discarding an earlier restriction. This is useful when an exact real number is described by increasingly precise bounds rather than by a finite decimal expansion. The bisection method, for instance, produces nested intervals that keep enclosing a zero of a function.
For a simple example, the closed intervals In​=[1−1/n,1+1/n] are nested and all contain 1. Their lengths 2/n tend to zero, so the nested interval theorem leaves exactly that point. The family Jn​=[1−1/n,2+1/n] is also nested, but its intersection is the whole closed interval [1,2]. Nesting alone does not force uniqueness.
The open intervals Kn​=(0,1/n) illustrate a different possibility. Every finite collection has a nonempty intersection, but the intersection of all of them is empty: any positive candidate eventually exceeds 1/n, and zero is excluded from every member. Each finite row in the diagram contains points; the full infinite family need not.
Nested interval theorem

Nested intervals OurBigBook.com
If I1​⊇I2​⊇⋯ are nonempty closed intervals with finite endpoints, then at least one real number belongs to every member. If their lengths tend to zero, exactly one real number belongs to every member. The result turns an unlimited sequence of consistent enclosures into an existence guarantee.
Write In​=[an​,bn​]. Nesting makes the left endpoints nondecreasing and the right endpoints nonincreasing. Their bounds give finite supremum and infimum, with
⋂n=1∞​In​=[supn≥1​an​, infn≥1​bn​].
(39)
Indeed, every bn​ is an upper bound for all the aj​, so the least-upper-bound property gives supj​aj​≤bn​ for every n. This proves the displayed interval is nonempty. If bn​−an​→0, its two endpoints must coincide. This is the connection to the completeness of the real numbers discussed in Günther Hörmann and David Langer, Einführung in die Analysis, §§3.15–3.16: nested intervals and order completeness.
The distinction between existence and uniqueness is useful in computation. If an unknown point x∗​ lies in every [an​,bn​], the midpoint mn​=(an​+bn​)/2 satisfies
∣mn​−x∗​∣≤2bn​−an​​.
(40)

Closedness and a finite initial enclosure matter. The open intervals (0,1/n) have no common point, while the closed but unbounded intervals [n,∞) also have empty intersection. A picture of a few intervals cannot certify the intersection of an infinite family; the hypotheses of the nested interval theorem do that work.

[a,b]={x∈R:a≤x≤b},a≤b.
(41)

Including the endpoints has a useful consequence for limits: a convergent sequence whose terms lie in [a,b] has its limit of a sequence in [a,b] too. Finite endpoints also make this a bounded set, so it is a compact set by the Heine-Borel theorem. These two properties support both the nested interval theorem and the extreme value theorem.

Extreme value theorem

Words: 500 Articles: 2
Real analysis OurBigBook.com
A real-valued function that is continuous on a nonempty compact space attains both a global minimum and a global maximum. In particular, for a continuous function f:[a,b]→R on a nonempty closed interval, there are points xmin​,xmax​∈[a,b] such that
f(xmin​)≤f(x)≤f(xmax​)for every x∈[a,b].
(42)
The important word is “attains”: the best values occur at actual allowed inputs, rather than merely being approached. The interval version is [ref].
For a worked example, take f(x)=(x−1)2 on [−1,2]. Its global minimum is f(1)=0, and its global maximum is f(−1)=4. Nonnegativity gives the first answer; ∣x−1∣≤2 on the specified closed interval gives the second. The endpoint x=−1 is essential: looking only for a zero derivative would find the minimum and miss the maximum.
For comparison, the continuous function g(x)=x on the open interval (0,1) has infimum 0 and supremum 1, but neither is a value of g. Even a closed domain is insufficient without continuity: define h(x)=x for 0≤x<1, and h(1)=0. On [0,1], its supremum is 1, approached by xn​=1−1/n for n≥2, but every function value is strictly less than 1. This endpoint change makes h discontinuous, preventing attainment. On the unbounded real line, the continuous function x↦x has neither a global minimum nor a global maximum. These examples show what can fail when a hypothesis is dropped; functions outside the hypotheses may still have extrema.
The extreme value theorem is an existence tool for optimization: first establish that a continuous objective function on a nonempty compact feasible set has a best value, then investigate where it occurs. It neither locates the optimizing point nor promises uniqueness or differentiability. For example, the absolute value function ∣x∣ on [−1,2] has its global minimum at zero although no derivative exists there; a constant function has every input as a minimizer. This role in optimization is explained in University of Toronto MAT237 notes, section 1.4: compactness and the extreme value theorem.
A short proof outline identifies the mechanism. The continuous image of a compact space is compact; a nonempty compact subset of the real line contains its infimum and supremum. For a closed interval, one can instead choose inputs whose outputs approach the supremum, extract a convergent subsequence by the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, and use continuity to make its limiting output equal that supremum. The closed interval retains the limiting input. Repeating the argument for the infimum supplies the minimum.

when the integral is finite. The exponent p controls how strongly large values influence the result. For a two-coordinate vector (3,4), treat the coordinates as a function on two inputs with counting measure. Then ∥(3,4)∥1​=3+4=7, ∥(3,4)∥2​=9+16​=5, and ∥(3,4)∥∞​=4. If e is an error function, its L1 norm measures aggregate absolute error, its L2 norm measures the square root of aggregate quadratic loss, and its L-infinity norm bounds error almost everywhere. Concentrating a large error on a set of small positive measure can give a modest finite Lp norm but a large L-infinity norm. The three-point example and diagram in L-infinity norm show this explicitly, including why a null set behaves differently from a rare event.

Sequence OurBigBook.com
A geometric progression is a sequence obtained by repeatedly multiplying by one fixed common ratio r:
a0​=a,an+1​=ran​,an​=arn(n≥0).
(58)
Here a and r may be real numbers or complex numbers. The recurrence is meaningful even when a=0 or r=0; expressing r as a ratio of successive terms requires a nonzero denominator. As a polynomial convention, r0=1, including at r=0.
For example, quantities 100,80,64,51.2,… retain four fifths of their preceding value at every step. The decrement changes, but the retained fraction does not. With the same initial value and common ratio 2, the terms are 100,200,400,800,…. This multiplicative structure is useful whenever the same proportional rule repeats: it turns many updates into the single exponentiation rn. An arithmetic progression instead repeats an additive increment.
For nonzero a, the modulus of an​ tends to zero when ∣r∣<1, stays fixed when ∣r∣=1, and grows without bound when ∣r∣>1. For a negative real common ratio, successive nonzero terms also alternate in sign. Thus the terms 1,−1/2,1/4,−1/8,… decay in size while crossing zero at every step. Adding the terms gives a geometric series; the individual terms and their accumulated partial sums are different sequences.

Sequence and series OurBigBook.com
A series adds the terms of a sequence in their specified order. Its infinite-sum notation is defined through finite partial sums:
SN​=∑n=1N​an​,∑n=1∞​an​=limN→∞​SN​

when the displayed limit of a sequence exists as a finite number. Otherwise the series is not a convergent series in the ordinary sense. Writing an infinite list of additions does not by itself assign it a finite sum. Cesàro summation is a different prescription, with its own definition.
Two positive series make the distinction concrete. For an​=1/n, the individual terms tend to zero but the harmonic series has unbounded partial sums. For an​=1/[n(n+1)], partial fraction decomposition reveals a telescoping series whose partial sums tend to one. The useful question is how much all the remaining terms can contribute together, rather than only how small the next term looks.

Summation method OurBigBook.com
Cesàro summation assigns a value to a series when the arithmetic means of its partial sums approach a finite limit of a sequence. Here we use the first-order method, often written (C,1). For a real or complex series beginning at index zero, define
sn​=∑k=0n​ak​,σN​=N+11​∑n=0N​sn​.
(71)
It is Cesàro summable to L when σN​→L. The averaging is applied to the partial sums sn​, rather than to the original terms an​. This distinction is essential: the terms can average to zero while their accumulated sum keeps growing. [ref]
For Grandi's series 1−1+1−1+⋯, the partial sums alternate between one and zero. The series is not a convergent series, but the two values occupy asymptotically equal proportions of the averaging window. In the declared index convention,
σ2m​=2m+1m+1​,σ2m+1​=21​,
(72)
so its first-order Cesàro sum is 1/2. This names a particular summation method; it does not turn the oscillating partial sums into an ordinarily convergent sequence.
Why is this useful? An oscillating approximation can retain stable information when its cumulative average settles. Because the Cesàro theorem for convergent sequences preserves an existing limit of a sequence, this adds some new cases without changing the sum of any ordinarily convergent series. For Fourier series, averaging the Fourier partial sums gives a Fejér sum; the existing Fejér kernel and approximation articles explain its effect on reconstruction. Averaging does not guarantee success for every oscillating sequence, as the bounded partial sums need not be Cesàro summable example shows.
One historical motivation was the multiplication of series. In 1918, A. F. Andersen recalled Ernesto Cesàro's product theorem and cited his 1890 publication at the start of a study of products involving Cesàro summable series. This connects the theory with preserving useful operations on sums, as well as with assigning a value to an isolated example. His paper treats several orders of summability; the examples here use only (C,1).[ref]

Factorial series OurBigBook.com
A factorial series with integral digits 0≤an​<n is an irrational number exactly when positive digits occur infinitely often and digits below their maximum occur infinitely often. Under these two conditions every scaled tail N!∑n>N​an​/n! lies strictly between zero and one. If the sum were a rational number A/B, choose N≥B; then N!A/B and the scaled finite head are integers, contradicting the strict tail bound. Conversely, an eventually zero digit sequence gives a finite rational number sum, and an eventually maximal sequence gives a finite head plus 1/N!, again a rational number.

The term test for divergence says that a series cannot converge if its terms fail to tend to zero. Indeed, if its partial sums satisfy Sn​→S, then an​=Sn​−Sn−1​→S−S=0. This is a necessary condition for a convergent series.
The converse fails: 1/n→0, but the harmonic series diverges. For a quick successful test, ∑n=1∞​n/(n+1) diverges because its terms tend to one. The test gives no conclusion for ∑1/n or ∑1/[n(n+1)]: both have terms tending to zero, yet only the second is a convergent series. Harmonic series (∑n=1∞​n1​)

Words: 441 Articles: 1
Series (mathematics) OurBigBook.com
The harmonic series is the positive series
1+21​+31​+41​+⋯=∑n=1∞​n1​.
(84)
Its partial sums are the harmonic numbers HN​. Although the individual terms tend to zero, HN​ grows without bound, so the harmonic series is not a convergent series. This is a basic warning against using the size of one term as a bound on all the terms still to come.
The growth is slow enough to be visually deceptive. The partial sums at N=10,100,1000,10000 are approximately 2.92896825,5.18737752,7.48547086,9.78760604. Adding ten times as many terms increases the accumulated total by roughly log10≈2.30258509, rather than multiplying the total by ten. The telescoping series ∑1/[n(n+1)] has similarly vanishing terms but approaches the finite sum one.
A short block argument proves the divergence without trusting a finite plot. For each integer k≥0, the block from 2k+1 through 2k+1 contains 2k terms, each at least 1/2k+1. Therefore
∑n=2k+12k+1​n1​≥21​,H2m​≥1+2m​.
(85)
Every doubling supplies at least another half, and arbitrarily many doublings are possible. A collection of tiny terms can still have a substantial combined contribution. See Jiří Lebl, Basic Analysis I, Example 2.5.11 for this grouping proof.
Integral comparison sharpens the growth estimate. Here log denotes the natural logarithm. Since 1/x is a strictly decreasing function for positive x, comparison of rectangles with the integral gives
log(N+1)≤HN​≤1+logN.
(86)
Thus the divergence is logarithmic. The finer difference HN​−logN tends to the Euler--Mascheroni constant, approximately 0.57721566; the harmonic number expansion supplies higher-order corrections. This turns the counterexample into a usable quantitative estimate of accumulated reciprocal contributions.
Euler's De progressionibus harmonicis observationes, written in 1734 and published in 1740, studies these sums beyond the yes-or-no question of convergence. Sections 2–3 compare long blocks to show continued growth, and later sections compare the sums with logarithms and calculate the constant offset. The [ref] identifies the dates and original publication; [ref] makes the calculations accessible. This is not a claim that Euler first discovered divergence: the paper's interest includes measuring how slowly a divergent sum grows.

A sequence (xn​)n≥1​ of real numbers has limit of a sequence L∈R, written xn​→L, precisely when
∀ε>0∃N∈N>0​∀n≥N:∣xn​−L∣<ε.

The absolute value measures the error. The tolerance ε is chosen first; N may depend on it, but must control every later term. Infinitely many accurate terms alone do not suffice. For example, xn​=(−1)n repeatedly equals one but also repeatedly differs from one by two. The definition and uniqueness of the limit of a sequence are discussed in MIT 18.100A, Lecture 6, definitions 13 and theorem 15.
For a worked error estimate, let xn​=3+2/n. Then ∣xn​−3∣=2/n, so any positive integer N>2/ε works. With ε=0.01, choose N=201; every later error is at most 2/201<0.01. The strict inequality matters: N=200 would give equality at its first term. A limit of a sequence turns the informal instruction “take enough terms” into an explicit accuracy guarantee.
The limit of a sequence is unique: two distinct proposed answers cannot both be within arbitrarily small error of every late term, by the triangle inequality. Changing finitely many initial terms does not change it. For an extended real number, xn​→+∞ means ∀M∈R∃N∀n≥N: xn​>M; convergence to −∞ similarly requires xn​<M. These describe escape rather than a finite answer. The extended-real Fekete lemma is an example where the limit of a sequence need not be finite.

The Cesàro mean of the first n≥1 terms of a sequence is their arithmetic mean. It is a cumulative average: increasing n includes the whole initial segment, rather than a fixed-length sliding window. For ak​=(−1)k, the even-length averages are zero and the odd-length averages are −1/n, so they tend to zero even though the sequence does not converge.

The full cycles contribute exactly M per term; the remainder contributes a fixed bounded error divided by n. Thus the Cesàro means tend to M. The cycle 0,2,1 in the bounded partial sums need not be Cesàro summable illustration has arithmetic mean one. Treating it as a sequence of partial sums gives a series with first-order Cesàro sum one; averaging a sequence and summing its terms remain different operations.

Pointwise convergence (fn​(x)→f(x))

Words: 459 Articles: 3
Sequence and series OurBigBook.com
For a sequence of functions fn​:X→R and a function f:X→R on the same domain of a function, pointwise convergence to f means
∀x∈X∀ε>0∃N∈N>0​∀n≥N:∣fn​(x)−f(x)∣<ε.
(92)
At each fixed input, this is the ordinary limit of a sequence. The index may depend on both the input and the requested accuracy: N=N(x,ε). It therefore certifies each input separately, with no promise about the worst error across the domain of a function. This is a useful first way to identify a candidate pointwise limit: hold the input still and study a numerical sequence. See MIT 18.100A, Lecture 23, definition 7.
Consider the polynomial functions fn​(x)=xn, with positive integer index n, on the interval [0,1]. For 0≤x<1 the geometric sequence (xn) tends to zero, while fn​(1)=1. Thus its pointwise limit is
f(x)={0,1,​0≤x<1,x=1.​
(93)
Each fn​ is a continuous function, but this pointwise limit fails continuity at one: its nearby values from the left are zero while its value at one is one. At any fixed 0<x<1 and 0<ε<1, the logarithm gives the sufficient choice N>log(ε)/log(x). For example, at x=1/2 and ε=0.01, N=7 works because 2−7=0.0078125, whereas 2−6=0.015625. As the input approaches one from below, the required index grows without bound. A common tolerance needs increasingly late indices at different inputs.
An even sharper warning concerns integration. On [0,1], define the continuous functions
gn​(x)=⎩⎨⎧​2n2x,2n−2n2x,0,​0≤x≤1/(2n),1/(2n)≤x≤1/n,1/n≤x≤1.​
(94)
Their supports are [0,1/n], with height n at 1/(2n) and value zero at both ends. Every fixed x>0 eventually lies beyond the support, and gn​(0)=0 always, so pointwise convergence gives the zero function. Nevertheless, each integral is the area of a triangle: ∫01​gn​(x)dx=21​(1/n)n=21​. Shrinking width exactly compensates increasing height. Hence the limit of these integrals differs from the integral of the pointwise limit; interchanging them requires additional conditions, such as uniform convergence preserves integrals on a compact interval.

A power series combines a sequence of coefficients with monomials in the displacement from a fixed centre:
∑n=0∞​an​(z−c)n.
(95)
The variable z, centre c, and coefficients can be real numbers or complex numbers. Its degree-N partial sum PN​(z)=∑n=0N​an​(z−c)n is a polynomial, so a convergent power series can turn a complicated function into increasingly accurate finite calculations. Convergence, and the error after stopping, are essential parts of that claim.
The geometric series supplies the simplest computed example:
1−z1​=1+z+z2+⋯,∣z∣<1.
(96)
At z=1/2, stopping after degree ten gives P10​(1/2)=1.9990234375, differing from the exact value 2 by 1/1024=0.0009765625. At z=0.99, the same degree gives only about 10.4662 instead of 100. The same formula has very different practical accuracy at different points; the geometric power-series remainder quantifies it.
The structure is useful beyond numerical evaluation. Within its radius of convergence, termwise differentiation of a power series turns a question about a derivative into a question about coefficients. A Taylor series chooses an​=f(n)(c)/n! when it represents the function locally. A formal power series instead uses the coefficients algebraically, without asserting numerical convergence; the existing generating function examples use that distinction to encode counting problems.

sup∣z∣≤r​​1−z1​−PN​(z)​≤1−rrN+1​.

Generating function (A(x)=∑n≥0​an​xn)

Words: 861 Articles: 1
Power series OurBigBook.com
A generating function packages a sequence into a series so that operations on objects become operations on their encodings. An ordinary generating function uses the power series A(z)=∑n≥0​an​zn; in counting problems, the coefficient an​ records the number of objects of size n. The variable z initially marks size: it need not be assigned a numerical value. Coefficient extraction writes this recovery as [zn]A(z)=an​. One compact expression can therefore answer infinitely many counting questions, while explaining how their answers fit together.
Start with two contributions: choose i from {0,1,2} and j from {0,1}, with exactly one option at each allowed value. Their individual ordinary generating functions are the polynomials P(x)=1+x+x2 and Q(x)=1+x. To count ordered pairs by total i+j, multiply:
P(x)Q(x)=(1+x+x2)(1+x)=1+2x+2x2+x3.
(99)
The coefficients 1,2,2,1 count the ways to obtain totals zero through three. For total two, the possibilities are (1,1) and (2,0); the two corresponding monomials both contribute x2. There are six ordered pairs altogether, agreeing with P(1)Q(1)=3⋅2=6.
If the first contribution has two distinguishable choices when i=1, replace P(x) by 1+2x+x2. Its product with Q(x) becomes 1+3x+3x2+x3. The coefficients now carry multiplicities as well as possible totals; the exponent still records cost. This lets the same construction handle several actions with identical costs without losing their separate identities.
In general, the Cauchy product gives
[zn](A(z)B(z))=∑k=0n​ak​bn−k​.
(100)
For each split of the total size, the rule of product counts the choices of the two components; summing over those splits counts all possibilities. This requires each combined object to have a unique decomposition into the two components. The same idea works for costs, lengths, or other additive measures, not just the number of pieces. See MIT 18.310, generating functions, sections 1–2.
Now cover a board of length n with tiles of lengths one and two, without gaps or overlaps. Let tn​ count these tilings. There is exactly one empty tiling, so t0​=1, and t1​=1. Removing the first tile leaves a board shorter by one or two, giving the recurrence relation
tn​=tn−1​+tn−2​(n≥2),(t0​,t1​,t2​,t3​,t4​,t5​)=(1,1,2,3,5,8).
(101)
These are the Fibonacci numbers shifted by one index: tn​=Fn+1​ under the convention F0​=0, F1​=1. Keeping the empty tiling is essential to both the counting rule and the resulting ordinary generating function.
For F(z)=∑n≥0​tn​zn, the empty board or a first tile followed by a remaining tiling gives
F(z)=1+(z+z2)F(z),F(z)=1−z−z21​=1+z+2z2+3z3+5z4+8z5+⋯.
(102)
Equivalently, F(z)=∑m≥0​(z+z2)m: each factor chooses one tile, and m counts pieces while the exponent of z records total length. The same ordinary generating function counts ordered histories of two repeatable actions costing one and two units. Histories (1,2) and (2,1) differ despite having the same total cost. MIT's notes use dots and dashes with these costs, including the empty message. [ref]
These identities hold in formal power series algebra: each requested coefficient uses only finitely many contributions. The repeated-choice expansion is legitimate because z+z2 has zero constant term; a zero-cost repeatable action would allow infinitely many histories of the same size. Numerical evaluation separately requires a convergent series. Here the radius of convergence is (5​−1)/2, the reciprocal of the golden ratio. At z=1, the rational function equals −1, but the counting series diverges: that value cannot represent its sum.
Other generating functions change the encoding: an exponential generating function divides by factorials, while a Dirichlet series uses n−s. A counting generating function also differs from a probability generating function, whose coefficients must be nonnegative and sum to one.
Exponential generating function (A(z)=∑n≥0​an​zn/n!)
Words: 313
Generating function OurBigBook.com
An exponential generating function encodes a sequence using A(z)=∑n≥0​an​zn/n!. For labelled counting, an​ is the number of structures on a fixed set of n distinct labels. Labels distinguish otherwise similar objects: changing which person belongs to a group can change the structure. Recover the count by coefficient extraction as an​=n![zn]A(z). The raw coefficient is an​/n!, not an​.
The factorial makes multiplication account automatically for distributing labels. To combine an A-structure on k labels and a B-structure on the remaining n−k, choose the first label subset in (kn​) ways, then choose the two structures. The binomial coefficient counts how the two groups of labels interleave within the full label set. Thus
A(z)B(z)=∑n≥0​cn​n!zn​,cn​=∑k=0n​(kn​)ak​bn−k​.
(103)
The normalization works because 1/(k!(n−k)!)=(kn​)/n!. This explains the usefulness of exponential generating functions for labelled counting: an ordinary Cauchy product would omit the choices of labels. See Peter Magyar, Math 482, notes for 2/7, labelled product principle.
For a concrete example, there is one undecorated set on any given collection of labels. Its exponential generating function is the exponential function E(z)=ez=∑n≥0​zn/n!. Combine a red set and a blue set, allowing either to be empty:
E(z)E(z)=e2z=∑n≥0​2nn!zn​.
(104)
Every label independently receives one of two colours, giving 2n assignments by the rule of product. With three labels, the counts by number of red labels are 1,3,3,1, totalling eight. Choosing only the two group sizes would give the four possibilities (0,3),(1,2),(2,1),(3,0); it would forget which labels are red.
Indeed, the ordinary generating function for the constant sequence an​=1 is the geometric series 1/(1−z). Its square has coefficient [zn](1−z)−2=n+1, counting pairs of nonnegative sizes. Both encodings are correct for their respective questions. The decision is whether identity matters when objects are combined.
For unordered sets of labelled components of positive size, an exponential generating function B(z) becomes eB(z): the term B(z)m/m! forgets the ordering of m components. The existing rooted-tree generating function develops the richer example T=zeT. A labelled rooted tree consists of its root of a tree and an unordered set of smaller labelled rooted trees, connecting the same label-distribution mechanism to recursive counting.

Radius of convergence (R)

Words: 1k Articles: 10
Power series OurBigBook.com
The radius of convergence of ∑n≥0​an​(z−c)n is the unique R∈[0,∞] separating interior absolute convergence from exterior divergence. It converges absolutely when ∣z−c∣<R and diverges when ∣z−c∣>R. At the centre it always has the finite value a0​, since all positive powers vanish. The boundary convergence of a power series is a separate question.
For 0<R<∞, the interior is a disk in the complex plane and an open interval (c−R,c+R) on the real line. A power series converges uniformly on every smaller closed disk ∣z−c∣≤r<R. This gives stable polynomial approximation over a whole compact region, rather than a separate limiting calculation at each point. See Jiří Lebl, Basic Analysis, §11.3.2: convergence of power series.
Four examples reveal what R measures:
  • ∑n≥0​zn has R=1, since its coefficients have constant magnitude one.
  • ∑n≥1​zn/n also has R=1: a factor 1/n changes boundary behaviour without changing the limiting coefficient-root growth.
  • ∑n≥0​zn/n! has R=∞. The ratio test gives successive term ratio ∣z∣/(n+1)→0 for every fixed z, producing the exponential function.
  • ∑n≥0​n!zn has R=0. For any z=0, successive term magnitudes have ratio (n+1)∣z∣→∞, so the terms do not tend to zero.
The Cauchy-Hadamard theorem computes R directly from the coefficients. The attractive feature is that one growth statistic decides convergence throughout the interior and exterior, including sparse series with many zero coefficients. Finite changes to the coefficients do not alter the radius, though they can change the sum.
Boundary convergence of a power series
Words: 199
Radius of convergence OurBigBook.com
Knowing the radius of convergence does not settle convergence on its boundary. The three power series
∑n=0∞​zn,∑n=1∞​nzn​,∑n=1∞​n2zn​
(106)
all have radius one, but behave differently on ∣z∣=1.
For the geometric series, boundary terms all have complex modulus one, violating the term test for divergence. For the second series, absolute values give the divergent harmonic series at every boundary point. At z=1 the series itself is harmonic and diverges. At any other point on the unit circle, its geometric partial sums obey
​∑k=1N​zk​=​1−zz(1−zN)​​≤∣1−z∣2​.
(107)
The Dirichlet test with the decreasing sequence 1/n→0 therefore gives conditional convergence. In particular, z=−1 gives the negative of the alternating harmonic series, with sum −ln2. For the third series, the convergent p-series ∑n≥1​1/n2 bounds the absolute values at every boundary point, giving absolute convergence by the comparison test for series.
At z=−1, the rational function 1/(1−z) is well defined and equals 1/2, yet its geometric series diverges there. A formula for a function and a particular series representation can have different domains. Likewise, applying termwise differentiation of a power series preserves the radius but need not preserve the boundary convergence.

Cauchy-Hadamard theorem (R−1=limsupn→∞​∣an​∣1/n)

For the power series ∑n≥0​an​(z−c)n, the Cauchy-Hadamard theorem gives
R1​=limsupn→∞​∣an​∣1/n,

with R=∞ when the limit superior is zero, and R=0 when it is infinite. Away from the centre, the root test explains the formula: the limit superior of the term roots at displacement z−c is ∣z−c∣/R, interpreted as zero for R=∞ and infinite for R=0. Values below one give absolute convergence; values above one imply that the terms fail to tend to zero. A value of one leaves the boundary question open. At the centre the series converges regardless of R.
For a2n​=1 and a2n+1​=0, the coefficient roots alternate between one and zero, so their ordinary limit does not exist. Their limit superior is nevertheless one, giving R=1 for ∑n≥0​z2n=1/(1−z2) inside the unit disk. A ratio of consecutive coefficients would be undefined at the zero coefficients; the root-limsup formula handles the gap directly.
In the first part of his 1892 study of functions given by Taylor series, Jacques Hadamard introduced an upper-limit formulation for sequences and used coefficient roots to determine the radius of convergence. Sections 4–6 separate finite positive, zero, and infinite root-growth cases; the later parts study singularities and continuation. See Hadamard, Essai sur l'étude des fonctions données par leur développement de Taylor, Journal de mathématiques pures et appliquées, fourth series 8 (1892), pp. 107–109. This original text explains the coefficient-growth question without implying that the study of power series began there.

For example, f(x)=x2(1+x) has leading Taylor term x2 and is positive on both sides of zero sufficiently nearby; g(x)=x3(1+x) has leading Taylor term x3 and changes sign there. A sequence of functions fn​:X→Y converges uniformly to f:X→Y, where Y is a metric space with metric d, precisely when
∀ε>0∃N∈N>0​∀x∈X∀n≥N:d(fn​(x),f(x))<ε.

For real numbers, use d(u,v)=∣u−v∣, the absolute value of the difference. The universal quantification over inputs and existential quantification of the index change order: pointwise convergence allows ∀x∀ε>0∃N(x,ε), whereas uniform convergence requires ∀ε>0∃N(ε)∀x. Every later approximation must meet the same prescribed accuracy everywhere. This is valuable when the input is unknown beforehand or changes with the approximation index. Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence; the converse fails. [ref].
For functions taking values in real numbers on a nonempty domain of a function, the supremum error is En​=supx∈X​∣fn​(x)−f(x)∣, allowing +∞. Then uniform convergence is equivalent to En​→0, using the supremum norm when the difference is a bounded function. A supremum need not be attained, so bounds ∣fn​(x)−f(x)∣<ε at every input give En​≤ε; applying them with ε/2 gives the strict bound needed for the limit of a sequence.
For an easy uniform convergence example, let hn​(x)=x/(n+1) on the interval [0,1], for integers n≥1. Its uniform limit is zero and its supremum error is exactly 1/(n+1), attained at x=1. For every ε>0, the explicit choice N=max{1,⌈1/ε⌉} works, where the ceiling function rounds upward: if n≥N then 1/(n+1)<ε. For ε=0.01, choose N=100, giving En​≤1/101≈0.00990099. This provides a finite stopping rule before the input is known.
For fn​(x)=xn and its pointwise limit on [0,1], the error is zero at one but approaches one as x→1 from below. Consequently
supx∈[0,1]​∣fn​(x)−f(x)∣=1
(117)
for every positive integer n. This supremum is not attained: at x<1 the error is xn<1, and at x=1 it is zero. Even deleting the endpoint leaves supremum error one on [0,1). The supremum error persists although every fixed input eventually becomes accurate. Indeed, xn​=2−1/n<1 gives error exactly 1/2 at every index. On the smaller interval [0,a], for any fixed 0≤a<1,
supx∈[0,a]​∣fn​(x)∣=an⟶0.

For a=0.8 and n=20, the exact bound is 0.820=0.01152921504606846976. A tolerance of 0.01 needs n≥21, since 0.821=0.009223372036854775808. Taking the logarithm gives n>log(0.01)/log(0.8)≈20.6377; the ceiling function gives 21 here because the ratio is not an integer. If the ratio were an integer, the strict tolerance would require the next integer. The domain of a function determines whether this approximation gives a common accuracy guarantee. [ref].
The uniform limit theorem explains why uniform convergence of continuous functions preserves continuity. Its proof is short: fix x and ε>0, choose one fN​ with supremum error below ε/3, and use its continuity to make ∣fN​(y)−fN​(x)∣<ε/3 for y close enough to x. The triangle inequality then gives ∣f(y)−f(x)∣<ε. The same fN​ must control both inputs. No compactness assumption is needed. [ref].
On a fixed finite interval [a,b], uniform convergence preserves integrals on a compact interval: if each fn​ is Riemann integrable, so is f, and ∣∫ab​fn​−∫ab​f∣≤(b−a)En​→0. For hn​(x)=x/(n+1) on the interval [0,1], the integral is 1/[2(n+1)]→0, agreeing with the integral of its zero uniform limit. [ref].
However, uniform convergence of functions does not imply convergence of their derivatives. On the interval [0,π], take qn​(x)=sin(nx)/n, using the sine function. Thus the derivatives fail even pointwise convergence, despite uniform convergence of the original functions. Here the derivatives mean those of the same formulas defined on the real line and then restricted to the interval [0,π]. To exchange differentiation and a limit of a sequence, additional control such as uniform derivative convergence with an anchored value is needed. [ref].

A Cauchy sequence is a sequence whose sufficiently late terms are all close to one another. In a metric space (X,d), the precise condition is
∀ε>0∃N∈N>0​∀m,n≥N: d(xm​,xn​)<ε.

For real numbers with their usual metric, d(xm​,xn​)=∣xm​−xn​∣. The useful feature is that the definition compares computed terms to other computed terms: it does not require an already known limit of a sequence. The one index N must control every pair of later indices, not merely successive terms. [ref].
For an explicit example, take qn​=1−2−n for n≥1. Its tail of a sequence beginning at N lies in [1−2−N,1), and for every m,n≥N,

Choose N with 2−N<ε to certify the entire future sequence. For ε=0.1, N=4 works because 2−4=0.0625. The limit of a sequence is one, but the pairwise bound establishes the Cauchy sequence property without first needing that answer. By contrast, an​=(−1)n is not a Cauchy sequence: arbitrarily late even integers and odd integers give values separated by two. [ref].
Tiny successive changes do not provide this guarantee. For the harmonic numbers Hn​=∑j=1n​1/j, the successive difference Hn+1​−Hn​=1/(n+1) tends to zero, but

It holds in the real numbers by completeness of the real numbers, but can fail in the rational numbers: the rational endpoints from the bisection method approaching 2​ are a Cauchy sequence with no rational limit of a sequence. The existing construction in completeness of the real numbers shows how this happens. A Cauchy sequence is always a bounded sequence; in R, boundedness gives a convergent subsequence by the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, and the pairwise condition forces the whole sequence to share its limit. Completeness of the real numbers

Words: 478 Articles: 2
Cauchy sequence OurBigBook.com
Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges to a real number. Explicitly, the condition
∀ε>0∃N∈N>0​∀m,n≥N:∣xm​−xn​∣<ε

implies the existence of L∈R with xn​→L. The hypothesis compares approximations with one another, without requiring a candidate answer. This makes completeness of the real numbers an existence principle: sufficiently consistent approximations cannot approach a missing destination. [ref].
The equivalent least-upper-bound property says that every nonempty set A⊆R bounded above has a supremum s∈R. Precisely, every x∈A satisfies x≤s, and for every ε>0 some x∈A satisfies s−ε<x. The second condition excludes any smaller upper bound. No largest element of A is required.
The rational numbers lack this property. The set A={q∈Q:q≥0, q2<2} contains one and has upper bound two, but has no supremum in Q. A proposed rational supremum s would have to satisfy s2=2: if s2<2, a sufficiently small rational increase still lies in A; if s2>2, a sufficiently small rational decrease remains an upper bound. The irrationality of the square root of two excludes equality. In R, its supremum is 2​. [ref].
Construct this square root by the bisection method, starting with rational bounds [l0​,u0​]=[1,2]. At each step square the midpoint and retain the half whose endpoints bracket two after squaring. The first four resulting intervals are [1,3/2], [5/4,3/2], [11/8,3/2], and [11/8,23/16]. After k steps, uk​−lk​=2−k and lk2​<2<uk2​. Both endpoint sequences are Cauchy sequences because every later endpoint remains in the current interval. Completeness of the real numbers gives a common limit of a sequence L; continuity of squaring gives L2=2. The midpoint approximates L with error at most 2−(k+1). Thus exact rational arithmetic produces certified accuracy while completeness of the real numbers supplies the exact answer.
Richard Dedekind approached completeness of the real numbers by filling gaps in the rational numbers with Dedekind cuts. In the preface to his 1872 Continuity and Irrational Numbers, he traced the problem to teaching differential calculus in 1858 and wanting arithmetic foundations for limits. His construction makes a missing boundary, such as 2​, into a number defined by the separation it produces among rational numbers. [ref].

Single-point changes preserve Riemann integrals

Words: 67
Riemann integration OurBigBook.com
Changing the value of a bounded Riemann-integrable function at one point preserves its Riemann integral. The difference is supported at that point: partitions isolating it in intervals of arbitrarily small total length make both Darboux sums tend to zero. Thus a nonnegative single-point spike can have zero integral without vanishing everywhere. Its indefinite integral is identically zero, so the fundamental theorem of calculus derivative identity can fail at the changed point despite differentiability of the primitive.

It exists and equals integration against the signed measure induced by g. Continuous vector-valued integrators are handled componentwise, which defines path signatures of continuous bounded variation paths.

Direct Riemann integrability

Words: 81
Riemann integral OurBigBook.com
A function g on [0,∞) is directly Riemann integrable when its upper and lower sums on an equal-width mesh are absolutely finite and converge to the same finite integral as the mesh width tends to zero. A locally absolutely continuous integrable function with integrable derivative has this property: the upper-minus-lower sum is bounded by mesh width times its total variation. The derivative bound therefore gives bounded variation as well as tail control. This stronger form of integrability is a hypothesis of the key renewal theorem.

Such sets illustrate how an uncountable set may have an integrable indicator function of zero integral.

Convex function (f(tx+(1−t)y)≤tf(x)+(1−t)f(y))

Words: 2k Articles: 31
Real analysis OurBigBook.com
A function f:C→R on a convex set C is a convex function if, for every x,y∈C and t∈[0,1],
f(tx+(1−t)y)≤tf(x)+(1−t)f(y).
(150)
Geometrically, a line segment joining two points of its graph of a function lies on or above that graph of a function. The convex set condition ensures that the intermediate input stays in the domain of a function. An affine function satisfies the defining inequality with equality.
For the quadratic function f(x)=x2, the inputs 1 and 3 have equally weighted arithmetic mean 2. Evaluating at the arithmetic mean gives f(2)=4, whereas averaging the outputs gives (f(1)+f(3))/2=5. Averaging first saves one unit in this example. More generally, direct expansion gives
tx2+(1−t)y2−[tx+(1−t)y]2=t(1−t)(x−y)2≥0.
(151)
This identity proves convexity and also shows exactly when its defining inequality is strict.
For a differentiable convex function, the tangent line in one dimension, or the corresponding supporting affine function in several dimensions, lies below the entire graph of a function. This is the subgradient inequality. The equivalent geometric statement is that the epigraph, consisting of points on or above the graph of a function, is a convex set. These characterizations are developed in Boyd and Vandenberghe's convex-function slides, sections 3.1–3.4.
Convexity does not require differentiability: the absolute value function ∣x∣ is a convex function with a corner at 0. When a function is twice continuously differentiable on an open interval, it is a convex function exactly when its second derivative is nonnegative throughout that interval. In several dimensions, the corresponding criterion on an open convex set is that its Hessian matrix is positive semidefinite everywhere. The domain of a function matters: x3 is a convex function on [0,∞), but not on all of R. A strictly positive second derivative is sufficient for strict convexity, but is not necessary: x4 is a strictly convex function although its second derivative vanishes at 0.
The usefulness of convexity is that local information can certify a global conclusion. Every local minimum of a convex function on a convex set is a global minimum: if a lower value existed elsewhere, the defining inequality would produce lower values arbitrarily close to the proposed local minimum. For a differentiable convex function on an open convex set, a zero gradient therefore certifies a global minimum. Strict convexity gives uniqueness when a global minimum exists; it does not supply existence by itself. These facts explain the role of convex functions in convex optimization.

A differentiable convex function finite on all of Rd satisfies the boundary condition vacuously. The cumulant-generating function log(r/(r−θ)) on θ<r has derivative (r−θ)−1 and is essentially smooth. Restricting its domain to θ<λ<r destroys this property. This distinction matters in the lower bounds of the Gärtner–Ellis theorem.

Convex quadratic function (21​xTHx+bTx+c)

Words: 52
Convex function OurBigBook.com
A convex quadratic function on Rn has the form q(x)=21​xTHx+bTx+c with a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix H. Its Hessian is H, and q(y)−q(x)−∇q(x)⋅(y−x)=21​(y−x)TH(y−x)≥0, proving convexity directly. A stationary point is a global minimum. On a compact polytope, a minimum either is stationary in the interior or minimizes a restriction to a boundary face.

Bounded convex functions are locally Lipschitz on an open ball (∣f(u)−f(v)∣≤L∥u−v∥)

Convex function OurBigBook.com
Let a real convex function satisfy ∣f∣≤M on the open unit ball of a normed space. For 4r=1−∥x∥, points u,v∈B(x,r) satisfy ∣f(u)−f(v)∣≤(M/r)∥u−v∥. Extend the segment from u through v to length 2r; its endpoint still lies in the domain, and convexity bounds the difference by 2M∥u−v∥/(2r). Reverse u,v for the opposite inequality. Unlike finite-dimensional local continuity theorems, this argument applies in arbitrary dimension because boundedness on a full neighborhood is assumed.

Negative part of a finite convex function is Lipschitz (∣f−(x)−f−(y)∣≤L∣x−y∣)

Words: 131
Convex function OurBigBook.com
For a finite convex function f:R→R, its negative part f−=max(−f,0) is globally Lipschitz continuous. The negative sublevel set is an interval. If bounded, local Lipschitz continuity of finite convex functions bounds the slopes on its closure. If it is a left ray, any negative slope there would force f positive far to the left by the supporting-line inequality; all slopes on that ray are therefore nonnegative and bounded above near its finite endpoint. For a right ray the analogous slopes are nonpositive and bounded below. If f is negative everywhere, convexity and boundedness above force it to be constant. These cases bound the slopes of f− globally, including its zero extension outside the interval. In particular, integrability of f(Z) implies integrability of the negative part of every fixed translate f(Z+x).

Convex function OurBigBook.com
An affine minorant of f is a function x↦⟨a,x⟩+b that is everywhere at most f(x). Every proper lower-semicontinuous convex function has such a minorant, by separating a point below its closed epigraph. Adding a positive quadratic then yields a coercive function, which establishes existence in proximal minimization.

Absolute value at a simple zero ((∣g∣)±′​(a)=±∣g′(a)∣)

Words: 89
Absolute value OurBigBook.com
Suppose a real function g is differentiable at a, with g(a)=0 and g′(a)=0. The derivative definition gives g(a+h)=g′(a)h+o(∣h∣). The reverse triangle inequality then implies
∣g(a+h)∣=∣g′(a)∣∣h∣+o(∣h∣).
(156)
Thus ∣g∣ has unequal one-sided derivatives, ∣g′(a)∣ on the right and −∣g′(a)∣ on the left. More generally, multiplication by a function w continuous at a with w(a)=0 gives right and left slopes w(a)∣g′(a)∣ and −w(a)∣g′(a)∣. This elementary expansion explains how a smooth oscillation can acquire infinitely many corners under the absolute value function, even after multiplication by a factor that makes it differentiable at an accumulation point.

Absolute value OurBigBook.com
Let the locations an​ be distinct and bounded, and let cn​>0 with ∑n​cn​<∞. The Weierstrass M-test gives locally uniform convergence of G, so the uniform limit theorem makes it continuous. The reverse triangle inequality bounds each term's difference quotient by cn​. Consequently a uniformly small tail permits passing each one-sided difference-quotient limit through the series. At every point outside the locations, G′(x)=∑n​cn​sgn(x−an​); at am​, the right derivative minus the left derivative is 2cm​>0. Thus the function has precisely the prescribed cusp locations, even when they accumulate at another point where the function remains differentiable.

For scalar minimizers of ∫F(Du) with F∈C2(Rn) and globally bounded uniformly positive Hessian matrix, no higher differentiability of F is needed for interior gradient Hölder continuity. The weak Euler-Lagrange equation is divDF(Du)=0. Difference quotients solve uniformly elliptic equations with coefficient matrices obtained by averaging D2F along gradient segments. The Caccioppoli inequality and difference quotient characterization give u∈Hloc2​. The Sobolev chain rule then gives div(D2F(Du)D(Dk​u))=0. The De Giorgi-Nash-Moser theorem makes each derivative Hölder continuous, with exponent depending only on dimension and the ellipticity ratio. This scalar conclusion should not be assumed for vector-valued elliptic systems.

The coefficients are uniformly elliptic and locally smooth. Apply the weak maximum principle on inner domains whose closures lie in the original domain, then let their boundary distances tend to zero. The common continuous boundary values make their boundary differences tend uniformly to zero, proving uniqueness without assuming global bounds on derivatives of the linearized coefficients.

Jensen's inequality (f(EX)≤E[f(X)])

Words: 596 Articles: 2
Convex function OurBigBook.com
Jensen's inequality says that applying a convex function to a weighted mean cannot exceed the same weighted mean of its outputs. For nonnegative weights wi​ with ∑i=1n​wi​=1 and inputs xi​ in a convex set,
f(∑i=1n​wi​xi​)≤∑i=1n​wi​f(xi​).
(162)
Nonnegative weights are essential: this is a convex combination, rather than an arbitrary affine combination. For two inputs it is precisely the defining inequality for a convex function; repeatedly grouping inputs gives the finite weighted version.
Take f(x)=x2, weights 1/4 and 3/4, and inputs 1 and 3. Their weighted mean is 2.5, so the two sides are
f(2.5)=6.25≤41​f(1)+43​f(3)=7.
(163)
The Jensen gap is 0.75. The inequality measures the effect of replacing distinct inputs by one representative input before applying a nonlinear function.
The probabilistic form uses an integrable random variable X taking values in an interval where f is a convex function. If f(X) is also an integrable random variable and EX belongs to that interval, then
f(EX)≤E[f(X)].
(164)
The direction reverses for a concave function. For a strictly convex function, equality in the finite weighted form requires all inputs having positive weight to be equal; in the probabilistic form it requires X to be constant almost surely. An affine function gives equality for any admissible distribution. [ref].
For the quadratic function f(x)=x2 and a random variable with a finite second moment, the difference between the two sides is exactly its variance:
E[X2]−(EX)2=Var(X)≥0.
(165)
Consider two equally likely values 2−d and 2+d. Their expected value stays at 2 as d increases, but their variance is d2. Thus the expected value of the square grows from 4 to 4+d2. For the exponential function, the same two-point distribution gives E[eX]=e2coshd, while eEX=e2. Both are examples of Jensen's inequality, but their Jensen gaps depend differently on the spread of the inputs.
Another useful choice is the concave function logx on positive inputs. Its version of Jensen's inequality gives ∑i​wi​logxi​≤log(∑i​wi​xi​). Applying the increasing exponential function shows that the weighted geometric mean cannot exceed the weighted arithmetic mean. For the equally weighted inputs 1 and 9, these are 3 and 5. This recovers the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality and illustrates how choosing one function can generate an entire family of bounds.
A short proof idea explains the probabilistic form. If f has a subgradient g at μ=EX, the supporting affine function gives f(X)≥f(μ)+g(X−μ). Taking the expected value cancels the linear term because E[X−μ]=0. This argument applies, for example, to finite convex functions on R; more general domains of a function need attention to endpoints and the existence of a subgradient.
Johan Jensen's 1906 paper “Sur les fonctions convexes et les inégalités entre les valeurs moyennes” is an early source for the connection between convex functions and inequalities for means. [ref].

Jensen gap (E[f(X)]−f(EX))

Words: 61
Jensen's inequality OurBigBook.com
The Jensen gap is the nonnegative difference E[f(X)]−f(EX) in Jensen's inequality, under its integrability assumptions. It quantifies how much applying a convex function before averaging differs from applying it afterward. For f(x)=x2 it is the variance of X; for an affine function it is zero. For general convex functions, it depends on both the function and the distribution of X, and is not determined by the variance alone.

The global-domain assumption matters at endpoints of restricted domains.

If a twice differentiable real function on R satisfies f′′(x)≤−c for some fixed c>0, then it has a unique global maximum. The mean value theorem shows that f′ is strictly decreasing, and that f′(x)+cx is nonincreasing. Hence f′(x)≤f′(0)−cx for x>0 and f′(x)≥f′(0)−cx for x<0. These inequalities force opposite derivative signs at the two ends. The intermediate value theorem supplies a unique zero of f′, at which f changes from increasing to decreasing. Merely having f′′<0 does not guarantee existence: f(x)=−e−x is increasing and approaches its unattained supremum zero.
